title: Yam Suph / Sea Crossing Environments
subtitle: Compare environmental proposal families without choosing an exact crossing point
summary: Three schematic environmental families make the geographic debate explorable while keeping the specific water body and crossing location unresolved.
disclaimer: Environmental/candidate reconstruction only. These views do not depict a proven Exodus crossing site, ancient shoreline, route, wind event, or recovered paleohydrology. The visual states are project-authored schematics; site-specific hydrology and coastline data require primary-source verification before release-quality reconstruction.

evidenceLegend.label: Environmental proposal
evidenceLegend.description: A broad geographic/environmental family discussed in historical reconstruction, not a discovered crossing location.

evidenceLegend.label: Unknown / disputed
evidenceLegend.description: The specific body of water, route, and crossing location remain unresolved in the atlas.

evidenceLegend.label: Schematic reconstruction
evidenceLegend.description: The visible marsh, shore, water, and terrain forms are interface schematics rather than site-specific scientific reconstructions.

periods.label: Exodus narrative context
periods.note: No precise archaeological date or crossing year is assigned by this scene.

panorama.alt: Schematic environmental comparison for Yam Suph proposal families

comparison.label: Yam Suph proposal families
comparison.intro: Switching views changes the environmental hypothesis being illustrated, not the atlas confidence. Each remains a proposal family rather than a crossing pin.

options.label: Eastern Delta / lake-marsh
options.summary: A family of reconstructions places the crossing among ancient lakes, lagoons, marshes, or channels east of the Nile Delta and toward the Suez approaches.
options.rationale: The existing Yam Suph record already preserves this as one historically discussed family and emphasizes that exact paleohydrology and route remain debated.
options.objections: The schematic water network shown here is not a mapped ancient shoreline. Exact channels, lake extents, chronology, and the narrative route are not established by this scene.

options.label: Gulf of Suez
options.summary: Some reconstructions relate Yam Suph to the northern Gulf of Suez or its approaches rather than a Delta lake-marsh system.
options.rationale: This is a distinct proposal family already retained in the v1 interpretation record; the biblical text alone does not resolve it.
options.objections: A gulf setting does not establish a precise shore, crossing line, camp, or date. Ancient coastal and hydrological conditions would need separately verified reconstruction data.

options.label: Farther east / Aqaba family
options.summary: Farther-east proposals move the crossing and subsequent itinerary substantially eastward, including models associated with the Gulf of Aqaba region.
options.rationale: The v1 atlas records farther-east proposals because they exist in the interpretive landscape, while explicitly refusing to treat them as established.
options.objections: These proposals require a substantially different route reconstruction. The schematic mountains and gulf are not evidence for a crossing and do not identify a particular shore.

hotspots.label: Ancient water landscape
hotspots.summary: Eastern-Delta proposals depend on reconstructing water bodies whose ancient extent and connections changed through time.

whyShown.evidence: The atlas preserves eastern-Delta lake and marsh proposals as one interpretive family.
whyShown.inference: Paleohydrology may help test route models, but this schematic marsh is not a scientific reconstruction.
whyShown.alternatives: Gulf of Suez and farther-east families remain visible in the same explorer.

hotspots.label: No exact route through the wetlands
hotspots.summary: Even within an eastern-Delta model, the narrative stations and crossing line cannot be converted into a recovered GPS path.

whyShown.evidence: Succoth, Etham, Pi-hahiroth, Baal-zephon, and the crossing water are not all securely identified.
whyShown.inference: A corridor can illustrate a model, but an exact line would overstate the evidence.
whyShown.alternatives: Different reconstructions place the sequence in different parts of the eastern frontier.

hotspots.label: Gulf setting is not a crossing pin
hotspots.summary: The Gulf of Suez view illustrates a proposal family, not an exact ancient shoreline or event location.

whyShown.evidence: A Gulf of Suez family is preserved in the v1 interpretation record.
whyShown.inference: A coastal/gulf environment can explain the geographic character of the proposal without selecting a crossing beach.
whyShown.alternatives: Eastern-Delta and farther-east proposal families remain separate.

hotspots.label: A substantially different itinerary
hotspots.summary: Moving the crossing farther east changes the distances and route assumptions that must be explained.

whyShown.evidence: The existing atlas notes that farther-east proposals require a substantially different route reconstruction.
whyShown.inference: Terrain and distance can be compared, but the scene cannot resolve the textual-geographic debate by itself.
whyShown.alternatives: The explorer intentionally keeps the other proposal families one tap away.

hotspots.label: What you see is schematic
hotspots.summary: Water, reeds, shoreline, mountains, and foreground forms are project-authored visual categories, not recovered ancient scenery.

whyShown.evidence: No verified paleohydrology, ancient shoreline, or site-specific visual dataset is bundled in Batch 2.
whyShown.inference: Schematic environments make proposal families understandable while preserving the boundary between visualization and evidence.
whyShown.alternatives: A later release can replace these layers only after scientific datasets and licenses are verified from primary sources.
